**300** of 300

Every construction project needs a **Quality Assurance and Quality Control** (QA/QC) system — method statements, **Inspection Test Plans (ITP)**, checklists, test reports, and registers. For infrastructure and industrial projects, a full QA/QC library runs to hundreds of templates per work package. InfraLens provides **300 QA/QC templates** organized by work family — Concrete, Steel & Rebar, Aggregates, Cement, Soil, Finishes, Formwork, Waterproofing, MEP, and more. Every template references the underlying **IS code** (IS 456, IS 516, IS 1786, IS 383, IS 2386, IS 4031) or IRC code, with acceptance criteria and test frequency per **IS 456 Clause 15**, **ISO 9001**, and NABL requirements.

## Most-used QA/QC templates

8 essentials

The 8 templates every construction QA/QC team runs daily — all Excel/PDF, IS-code mapped.

[Pre-Pour Concrete Checklist\\
\\
Rebar, formwork, cover, embedded items, joint preparation — signed before every concrete pour. Hold point.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/concrete/pre-pour-inspection-checklist) [Concrete Cube Test (IS 516)\\
\\
Cube sample prep, curing, 7/28-day compression test. Frequency per IS 456 Clause 15 (1 set per 50 m³).](https://infralens.in/qaqc/concrete/cube-casting-compression-test-report) [Rebar / TMT Bar Inspection\\
\\
MTC, ISI mark, bend test, weight tolerance, cover verification per IS 1786:2008.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/steel/rebar-receiving-inspection-checklist) [Cement Physical Tests\\
\\
Fineness, consistency, setting time, compressive strength per IS 4031 — 1 sample per 100t of cement.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/cement/cement-physical-tests-report) [Aggregate Sieve Analysis\\
\\
Fine and coarse aggregate grading per IS 2386 Part 1 and IS 383:2016 — flakiness, elongation, deleterious.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/aggregates/aggregate-sieve-analysis-report) [NCR (Non-Conformance Report)\\
\\
Standard NCR format with classification (minor/major/critical), disposition, corrective and preventive action.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/generic/non-conformance-report-ncr) [Inspection Test Plan (ITP)\\
\\
Per-activity ITP with frequency, acceptance criteria, responsibility, H/W/R hold points — the QA/QC backbone.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/generic/inspection-test-plan-itp) [Slump Test (IS 1199)\\
\\
Workability test format — slump value, cone details, batch info. Frequency per batch or per 5 m³ — site-conditional.](https://infralens.in/qaqc/concrete/slump-workability-test-report)

## What is QA/QC in civil construction and why templates matter

**Quality Assurance (QA)** and **Quality Control (QC)** are the two complementary halves of construction quality management. QA is \*process-oriented\* — it's about setting up systems, procedures, and documentation to ensure quality can be achieved consistently (method statements, inspection plans, training, audits). QC is \*product-oriented\* — it's about actually verifying that individual work items meet specifications (cube tests, sieve analysis, rebar inspection, finish checks).

Every civil project of any significance has a QA/QC plan — mandated by the contract, enforced by the client or PMC consultant, and audited by regulatory bodies. For residential and small commercial work, it's often light (material test certificates, cube test reports, snag lists). For infrastructure (bridges, highways, dams, high-rise) and industrial projects (refineries, power plants), it's extensive — hundreds of checklists, test formats, and registers per work package.

InfraLens provides **300 QA/QC templates** organized by work family (Concrete, Steel, Aggregates, Cement, Soil, Finishes, Formwork, Piling, Waterproofing, Painting, Electrical, Plumbing, Fire Safety, HVAC, Bridges, Tunnels, Ports, Highways, Roofing, etc.). Every template references the relevant **IS code** or **IRC code** — e.g., concrete cube test format references IS 516:2021, sieve analysis references IS 2386 Part 1, TMT bar inspection references IS 1786. Templates are in Excel (with formulas and dropdowns) and PDF (print-ready for field use).

## How to use QA/QC templates effectively on your project

Start by mapping the templates you need against your project's scope: make a list of all work packages (excavation, PCC, RCC, masonry, plaster, tile, steel erection, painting, waterproofing, MEP), then pull the relevant checklists, test formats, and registers for each. A residential building typically needs 30-50 templates; a commercial highrise 80-120; a bridge project 150+; a large industrial project 200+.

The three **core template types**: (1) **Checklists** — pre-pour concrete, pre-shotcrete rebar check, formwork alignment, brick layer inspection — used by site supervisors before or after an activity. (2) **Test Reports** — cube compression (IS 516), slump test (IS 1199), sieve analysis (IS 2386), cement consistency (IS 4031) — filled by the lab technician, signed by QC engineer. (3) **Registers** — concrete pour log, material inward, NCR register, test report summary — cumulative records maintained throughout the project.

**Best practice**: start each work package with the checklist, use the test format whenever a test is conducted, update the register daily/weekly. Share monthly summaries with the PMC/client. Close out every NCR raised. Keep the QA/QC file current and accessible — during ISO audits or client inspections, a well-maintained QA/QC file tells 80% of the quality story.

## Frequently Asked Questions

12 common questions about this topic, answered by civil engineers.

What's the difference between QA and QC?+

**QA (Quality Assurance)** is process-focused — ensuring the systems exist to deliver quality. Activities: writing method statements, training workers, inspection test plans (ITP), internal audits, management reviews. **QC (Quality Control)** is product-focused — actually testing and inspecting the work. Activities: cube tests, dimensional checks, finish inspection, material test reports. QA prevents defects; QC detects defects. A good project has both — strong processes (QA) plus thorough inspection (QC). ISO 9001 is the global standard for quality management systems that governs both.

Which IS code specifies concrete cube test frequency?+

**IS 456:2000 Clause 15** and **IS 516:2021** together govern concrete quality testing. Cube test frequency per IS 456 Clause 15.2.1: 1 set of 3 cubes per 1 m³ up to 5 m³, then 1 set per 5 m³ up to 25 m³, then 1 set per 25 m³ up to 50 m³, then 1 set per 50 m³ up to 100 m³, then 1 set per 100 m³. Cubes tested at 28 days (also 7 days for intermediate check). Acceptance criteria: individual cubes >0.85×fck + 3 MPa; mean of 4 consecutive cubes >fck + 3 MPa (M15-M20) or fck + 4 MPa (M25+).

What is an Inspection Test Plan (ITP)?+

An **ITP** is a document that lists every inspection and test required for a specific work package, the frequency, the acceptance criteria, who carries it out, and who verifies/witnesses. Columns typically: activity, specification reference (IS code clause), inspection method, frequency, acceptance criteria, responsibility (contractor/consultant/third-party lab), record format (the test report template used), hold points (H = mandatory witness by consultant), review points (R = consultant reviews records). ITPs are the backbone of any QA/QC plan — a typical civil ITP might have 100-200 line items for an RCC building.

What is a hold point and a review point in an ITP?+

**Hold Point (H)**: work cannot proceed past this point without the consultant/client present for inspection. Example: pre-pour rebar inspection before concrete is cast — if the consultant isn't there, the pour is delayed. Hold points are for critical, irreversible steps. **Review Point (R)** or **Witness Point (W)**: consultant reviews records after the fact (not in real-time). Example: reviewing cube test reports in monthly meeting. **Information Point (I)**: contractor informs consultant but no action required. Hold points are the strongest control; they're used sparingly for high-impact quality gates.

Which IS code is used for steel reinforcement inspection?+

**IS 1786:2008** — the TMT bar specification — has the acceptance criteria: Fe 415 UTS 485 MPa, yield 415 MPa, elongation 14.5% min; Fe 500 UTS 545 MPa, yield 500, elongation 12% min; Fe 500D UTS 565 MPa, yield 500, elongation 16% min (ductile, for seismic zones III-V). Inspection checklist: manufacturer's test certificate (MTC), ISI mark, rolling mark visible, bar size by weight (IS 1786 Table 3 tolerances), surface condition (no rust flakes), bend test per IS 1599, rebend test per IS 1786. Sample 1 set per 25-30 tonne delivery lot.

What should be checked before a concrete pour?+

Our **pre-pour checklist** covers: (1) Rebar — diameter, spacing, cover, lap position, lap length, binding wire, cleanliness (no rust/oil/grease); (2) Formwork — alignment, plumb, level, tightness, release agent applied, inspection holes accessible; (3) Embedded items — plumbing sleeves, electrical conduits, anchor bolts, dowels — confirmed per drawings; (4) Construction joint preparation — roughened, cleaned, kept wet, pre-bonding agent applied; (5) Concrete placement — mix design approved, slump test equipment ready, cube mould ready, vibrator checked, curing material on standby; (6) Weather — no rain forecast, temperature 5-35°C. Signed by site engineer + consultant. Checklist is a hold point — pour doesn't start until it's green.

What is a Non-Conformance Report (NCR) and how do I manage one?+

An **NCR** is raised when work is found not in conformance with specifications — cube test fail, rebar cover less than specified, dimensional deviation outside tolerance, wrong finish. NCR workflow: (1) Raise — site supervisor or consultant identifies non-conformance, writes NCR with description, references, photos, (2) Classify — minor (rework easy, no structural impact), major (rework required, schedule impact), critical (removal/redo), (3) Disposition — accept as-is (with concession), rework, repair, reject/remove, (4) Corrective action — fix the immediate issue, (5) Preventive action — fix the root cause (training, revised method, better supervision), (6) Close-out — consultant signs off. All NCRs tracked in the **NCR Register** with open/closed status.

What tests are done on cement before use?+

Per **IS 4031** (Methods of Physical Tests for Hydraulic Cement — 15 parts) and **IS 4032** (Chemical Analysis): (1) Fineness (Blaine's method, IS 4031 Part 2) — min 225 m²/kg for OPC 33, 225 for 43, 370 for 53; (2) Standard consistency (IS 4031 Part 4); (3) Setting time (initial not less than 30 min, final not more than 600 min); (4) Compressive strength of mortar cubes at 3, 7, 28 days per grade; (5) Soundness (Le Chatelier method, IS 4031 Part 3); (6) Heat of hydration (for low-heat cement); (7) Chloride content (max 0.05% per IS 456). Sample 1 per 100 tonnes of cement delivery.

Which IS codes are used for aggregate testing?+

**IS 2386** — Methods of Test for Aggregates — has 8 parts: Part 1 (particle size & shape — sieve analysis, flakiness, elongation), Part 2 (estimation of deleterious materials), Part 3 (specific gravity, density, voids, water absorption, bulking), Part 4 (mechanical properties — abrasion, impact, crushing value), Part 5 (soundness), Part 6 (measuring mortar making properties), Part 7 (alkali-aggregate reactivity), Part 8 (petrographic examination). **IS 383:2016** — Coarse and Fine Aggregates for Concrete — specification: grading zones, deleterious limits, crushing value ≤30%, impact ≤30%, abrasion ≤30%. Test frequency: 1 set per 50 m³ of aggregate or per source change.

Are these templates compliant with ISO 9001 and NABL requirements?+

The templates follow ISO 9001:2015 principles (process approach, risk-based thinking, traceability, document control) — they can be used as-is within an ISO 9001 quality management system. Individual test format templates capture the data required by **NABL** (National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories) for accredited lab reports: sample identification, test method reference (IS code + clause), environmental conditions, equipment calibration status, result and uncertainty, signatures. For formal NABL accreditation of your in-house lab, additional documentation (quality manual, procedures, SOPs, calibration records) is required beyond what the templates cover.

How are the 300 templates organized?+

Templates are organized by **family** (work package): Concrete (~60 templates), Steel & Reinforcement (~25), Aggregates (~20), Cement (~15), Soil & Earthwork (~25), Formwork & Shuttering (~15), Brickwork & Masonry (~20), Plastering (~15), Flooring & Tiling (~15), Painting & Finishes (~15), Waterproofing (~10), MEP — Electrical & Plumbing (~25), Fire Safety (~10), Bridges — Specific (~15), Roads & Pavement (~15), Piling (~10), Others (~20). Each family has checklists, test formats, and registers. The total adds up to ~300 templates. Filter by family on the /qaqc page.

Do the QA/QC templates work for international projects?+

The templates are based on Indian Standards (IS) and MoRTH specifications — they work directly on Indian projects. For international projects using ASTM, EN, BS, or AS/NZS standards, the **format** (checklist/test/register structure) is universally applicable, but the **specific acceptance criteria and test methods** need to be mapped to the contract-specified code. Our templates show the IS code reference clearly so you can identify what to replace (e.g., "Concrete cube test per IS 516:2021" becomes "Concrete cube test per ASTM C39" on an ASTM-referenced project). The structural logic of the template doesn't change.
